abstract: Background: Finely tuned gamma (FTG) is a narrowband oscillation associated with dopaminergic ON states and dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease (PD), although its physiological significance remains debated. While deep brain stimulation (DBS) can entrain gamma oscillations, whether noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG across motor circuits remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed local field potentials recorded using sensing-enabled DBS systems in two cohorts of patients: 17 with subthalamic nucleus (STN) and 10 with globus pallidus internus (GPi) electrodes. Theta-burst transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tbTUS) targeted the primary motor cortex (M1) or GPi. FTG was assessed before, during, and up to 45 minutes after sonication. Associations with beta activity, levodopa-equivalent daily dose (LEDD), and dyskinesia were also examined. Results: FTG was detected in eight STN patients and one GPi patient, with five exhibiting reproducible peaks suitable for longitudinal analysis, broadly consistent with previous reports of intermittent FTG expression. M1 sonication reduced STN FTG in three patients, whereas GPi sonication increased STN FTG in one but did not significantly alter locally recorded GPi FTG in another. Finger-tapping-related FTG responses were heterogeneous. Resting FTG was not significantly correlated with beta activity or LEDD. However, dyskinesia was more frequent in sessions with detectable FTG than in those without (47% vs. 20%), although this association was not statistically significant (p = 0.067). Conclusions: These findings suggest that noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG in a circuit-dependent manner, distinct from DBS-induced gamma entrainment. FTG may provide a complementary electrophysiological biomarker alongside beta oscillations, potentially capturing additional aspects of motor-network activity and dyskinesia. Combining noninvasive TUS with intracranial DBS sensing may offer a useful approach for investigating FTG and its potential application in future adaptive DBS and individualized neuromodulation strategies.
